title: Customer success manager

manager.name: Priya
manager.title: Head of Customer Success
manager.persona_note: Priya has had disappointing experiences with recruiters, which is fair. A good recruiter earns trust with sharp questions, not promises.

teaser: Priya runs customer success at a software company and isn't sure a recruiter can help.
context: The company sells booking software to clinics and gyms and has about 80 people.
The new hire will report to Priya and join a team of four.
message: I need a customer success manager. Honestly, recruiters haven't helped much before.
The job ad is from last year. Can we talk for 10 minutes?
ad: 5 or more years in customer success
Must have managed 100 or more accounts
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Priya will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to keep big customers from leaving, with fewer but larger accounts.
needs.n2: Someone to welcome lots of small new customers quickly.
needs.n3: Someone to build and lead a support team.

beats.label: Past searches
beats.sam: I'll be honest. The last two recruiters I worked with sent me people who were all wrong for this.

choices.text: I'm sorry to hear that. What was it about those candidates that made them the wrong fit?
choices.reply: They'd all handled hundreds of tiny accounts. That's not what we do here.
choices.why: Asking what went wrong shows you're listening, and it tells you exactly what to avoid this time.

choices.text: Would it help if I walked you through how my process is different from the recruiters you worked with before?
choices.reply: Maybe. I've heard that before.
choices.why: Explaining your process is easy, but a manager who's been let down needs to see that you understand the problem first.

choices.text: Do you think the brief they were given was clear enough?
choices.reply: The brief was fine.
choices.why: Questioning their brief puts the manager on the defensive, which is the opposite of what you want early on.

choices.text: What would a great person get done in their first three months?
choices.reply: Visit our 25 biggest customers and spot who's unhappy before they decide to leave.
choices.why: An open follow-up turns a frustration into a clear picture of success.

choices.text: So you're looking for someone more senior than the people you saw?
choices.reply: Not more senior. Different.
choices.why: A leading guess narrows the answer. An open question would have given you the full picture.

choices.text: Were the people you met really that far off?
choices.reply: Yes, they were.
choices.why: Questioning the manager's judgment costs trust, and you don't learn anything new about what they need.

beats.label: Why it's open
beats.sam: I don't think I need to explain the job much. It's pretty straightforward.

choices.text: That makes sense. What's prompting the hire right now? Is something happening with customers?
choices.reply: Big customers are leaving after their first year, because nobody checks in until renewal time.
choices.why: Even a straightforward job is open for a reason. Asking why now usually uncovers what the hire really has to solve.

choices.text: Should I work from the standard customer success profile, then?
choices.reply: Yes, that's fine.
choices.why: Going with a standard profile saves time now, but you'd be guessing at what matters most for this team.

choices.text: In my experience, most searches go wrong because the job isn't explained properly. Couldn't that be what happened before?
choices.reply: Not this one.
choices.why: Even if it's often true, saying it to a manager who is already frustrated only confirms their doubts about recruiters.

beats.label: The must-have
beats.sam: They must have managed 100 accounts. It says so in the ad.

choices.text: How many accounts will this person actually look after?
choices.reply: About 25, but they're our biggest ones.
choices.why: Checking a must-have against the real job shows that 100 small accounts is the wrong kind of experience here.

choices.text: Should I screen for 100 or more accounts, then?
choices.reply: Yes, that's right.
choices.why: It sounds reasonable, but you'd be screening for the wrong kind of experience.

choices.text: So more accounts means more experience, right?
choices.reply: I suppose so.
choices.why: A leading question locked in a requirement that doesn't fit the job.

beats.label: Shortlist
beats.sam: Just send me ten resumes and I'll sort it out myself.

choices.text: Happy to. Would it help if I added a short note on each one, so you can sort them faster?
choices.reply: That would actually help a lot.
choices.why: Agreeing to a fair request, and making it easier, is how you rebuild trust after past letdowns.

choices.text: Would you rather see a smaller number of stronger candidates?
choices.reply: No, I'd like to see ten.
choices.why: A fair question, but it argued with a reasonable request. Sometimes going along with it is the better move.

choices.text: Ten is quite a lot to review on top of everything else. Could I just send you my top three instead?
choices.reply: That's what the last recruiter said.
choices.why: Pushing back on a small request spends trust you'll need later in the search.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: Pay is whatever's normal for this kind of job.

choices.text: So I only bring you people you can afford, what range has been approved?
choices.reply: $85,000 to $100,000 base salary, and it's approved.
choices.why: Linking the question to their goal makes the range easy to share.

choices.text: It's hard to start without a number. Could we pin one down first?
choices.why: You got the range, but the pressure cost some goodwill. Tying it to their goal works better.

choices.text: Is it okay if we figure out pay once we see who's interested?
choices.reply: Sure.
choices.why: Without a range, you can't tell which people the manager can actually afford.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Office days
beats.sam: They'll be in the office on Tuesdays. That's about it.

choices.text: One day a week is easy to explain. What happens on Tuesdays, so I can describe it to candidates?
choices.reply: It's our team day. We go through every big customer together.
choices.why: Accepting a reasonable request, then asking what happens on those days, shows curiosity and gives you a real selling point for candidates.

choices.text: Could that day be flexible for the right person?
choices.reply: No, Tuesday is our team day.
choices.why: It's a fair question, but asked before you understand why those days matter, it can sound like you're already negotiating against the manager.

choices.text: Most people I talk to want to be fully remote. Could we drop the office day?
choices.reply: Then they can apply somewhere else.
choices.why: Pushing to change a settled decision, with nothing to back it up, spends goodwill you'll need for the questions that actually change the search.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: Honestly, anyone friendly could do this job.

choices.text: What would make a great customer success manager choose this job over others?
choices.reply: They'd own our biggest customers and have a real say in the product.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive gives you the story to tell the right people.

choices.text: So I should look for people who are great with customers?
choices.reply: Exactly.
choices.why: Being good with people matters, but it won't stop a big customer from leaving. You'd miss what makes this job different.

choices.text: Isn't it a bit more complex than being friendly?
choices.reply: Now you sound like the last recruiter.
choices.why: Correcting the manager rarely changes their mind. A question about the job does.

candidates.name: Jesse
candidates.job: Customer success manager at a software company
facts: Saved 6 big accounts that planned to leave

reason.n1: Looks after a few big customers, stays in touch all year, and has saved six that planned to leave. That's what Priya needs, and it fits the range.

view.n1: Jesse is the one I'd trust with our biggest customers.

candidates.name: Reese
candidates.job: Customer success manager at an HR software company
facts: Focuses on customers around renewal time

reason.n1: Handles big accounts well, but focuses on them around renewal time. Priya said that's exactly why big customers are leaving.

view.n1: Reese would call our customers once a year. That's our problem now.

candidates.name: Casey
candidates.job: Account manager at a phone company
facts: Answers every email within an hour

reason.n1: The 150 accounts match the old ad, but Priya confirmed the job is 25 of the biggest customers, which needs much deeper attention.

view.n1: Casey's lovely, but our biggest customers need more time.

candidates.name: Tobi
candidates.job: Customer success director at a well-known software company
facts: Leads a team of 12 customer success managers
Presents to the company's leadership every quarter

reason.n1: The most impressive resume, but the job is hands-on: visiting 25 big customers and spotting trouble early. Tobi has been leading a team, not doing that work.

view.n1: Tobi would want a team to lead. I need someone in the room with customers.
